overview: This two-page Department of State list of papers indexes records concerning electric power in Japan from 1932 through 1938. It traces the industry's financial difficulties, inquiries into rural electrification, political debate over state control and nationalization, the Diet's enactment of electric-power legislation, and the resulting laws, ordinances, and administrative bodies. It also identifies a related Sino-Japanese conflict report concerning the planned destruction of a Chinese-Japanese power substation at Tsingtao and supplies cross-references to other decimal-file records.

subfiles.title: Department of State List of Papers: Electric Power—Japan, entries 18–28
subfiles.about: An index to diplomatic reports and related materials on Japan's electric-power industry, rural electrification, state control legislation, and a power installation at Tsingtao.
subfiles.summary: The first page records a 1932 assessment that the Japanese electric industry might meet its obligations only by reducing dividends, followed by a Rural Electrification Administration inquiry and an embassy response transmitting a Tokyo consular report on rural electricity. Subsequent entries index Dickover's 1936 reports on state control, nationalization, press commentary in the Tokyo Nichi Nichi, and a compromise based on Communications Minister Tanomogi's private-ownership, state-operation plan. A Tsingtao telegram reports Chinese plans to destroy a jointly Chinese-Japanese electric substation during the Sino-Japanese conflict while leaving the old plant operating. The remaining entries cover Grew's reports on the Diet's electric-power control legislation, the creation of a government-regulated power company, translations of pertinent laws, formation of the Electric Power Deliberative Commission, and implementing ordinances.

interest: The index outlines Japan's rapid movement from a financially strained, privately owned utility system toward centralized state direction during the 1930s. Its sequence is especially useful for locating contemporary diplomatic analysis, translated legislation, newspaper coverage, and administrative ordinances relating to that transformation. The Tsingtao entry adds a distinct wartime dimension by showing electrical infrastructure becoming a target during the Sino-Japanese conflict, while the decimal-file cross-references point researchers toward related records not contained in this excerpt.
